title: What is arthritis? Types, symptoms and treatment
description: Understand the main types of arthritis, symptoms, urgent warning signs, diagnosis and treatment. Find UK guidance on getting assessed and everyday support.
h1: What is arthritis? Types, symptoms and next steps
answer: Arthritis causes pain, swelling or stiffness in one or more joints. It is not one diagnosis: osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and gout have different causes and treatments. See a GP for unexplained joint symptoms that do not go away in a few days. Sudden severe pain or swelling, or a hot joint, needs urgent advice.
note: Prepared by Living With Arthritis after checks against the NHS and NICE sources listed below. This revised text is awaiting Louis Maxwell's final clinical review. No independent clinical review is claimed. A publication approval is not a separate independent review.

sections.heading: What happens in a joint?
paragraphs: A joint is where bones meet. Cartilage helps the ends of bones move smoothly. The joint lining and surrounding tissues also help support movement. Different types of arthritis affect these tissues in different ways. The location of pain alone cannot tell you the type of arthritis or rule out another cause.

Arthritis can affect hands, feet, knees, hips, the back or other joints. It can affect people of different ages, including children. Symptoms may vary, and a flare means they have become worse. A new hot or very painful joint should not automatically be treated as your usual flare.

sections.heading: How do the main types differ?
paragraphs:
- Osteoarthritis is the most common type in the UK. Changes in cartilage and other joint tissues can cause pain, stiffness and difficulty moving. Knees, hips and small hand joints are often affected. Symptoms do not necessarily keep getting worse.
- Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks joint tissues. It often affects small joints of the hands and feet. Early assessment and treatment matter because treatment can reduce joint damage.
- Gout is linked to uric acid crystals in and around a joint. It can cause sudden severe pain, heat and swelling. Do not assume a first hot, swollen joint is gout without assessment, because infection can cause similar symptoms.
- Other types include psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Lupus can also cause joint symptoms. A clinician can help identify the cause rather than relying on a symptom list.

sections.heading: When should you get urgent help?
paragraphs: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if you have sudden severe pain and swelling in one joint, or the skin around a joint is hot or red. Redness may be harder to see on brown or black skin. Sore joints with a high or low temperature, shivering or feeling unwell also need urgent advice. Not everyone with a joint infection has a fever.

The NHS also advises urgent assessment for joint pain that does not improve with painkillers, sore joints with eye pain or vision problems, or sore joints with pain when passing urine, genital discharge, or genital sores or a rash. Do not wait for an exercise programme or a routine scan if urgent signs are present.
In England, Scotland and Wales, call 111 where appropriate. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: When should you book a routine appointment?
paragraphs: See a GP for unexplained joint pain, swelling or stiffness that does not go away in a few days. Explain which joints are affected, whether you can see swelling, how long stiffness lasts and what has become harder to do. Do not wait until you cannot work or until symptoms are severe.

Suspected persistent inflammation of the joint lining needs specialist assessment. NICE recommends urgent referral in specified circumstances, including small hand or foot joints, more than one affected joint, or a delay of three months or more before seeking advice. Normal inflammatory markers or negative rheumatoid-factor or anti-CCP tests do not remove that referral need. Tests ordered in primary care should not delay referral.

sections.heading: How is arthritis diagnosed?
paragraphs: A healthcare professional asks about symptoms and medical history and examines the joints. Depending on the suspected cause, tests may include blood tests, an X-ray or ultrasound, or a sample of joint fluid. Not everyone needs all of these tests.

Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed from the history and examination without imaging. NICE describes a typical clinical pattern in people aged 45 or over with activity-related pain and no morning stiffness, or stiffness lasting no longer than 30 minutes. Different or unusual features may need further investigation. A scan or single blood result is not a complete diagnosis by itself.

sections.heading: What treatment can help?
paragraphs: Treatment depends on the type of arthritis, other health conditions and how daily life is affected. Options may include exercise or physiotherapy, occupational therapy for everyday activities, medicines, suitable aids and, for some people, surgery. Ask what each treatment is intended to do and how it will be reviewed.

For osteoarthritis, NICE identifies tailored therapeutic exercise and weight management, when appropriate, as core treatments alongside information and support. Medicines need an individual check of benefits and risks. NICE does not recommend glucosamine or hyaluronan injections for osteoarthritis. Corticosteroid injections may be considered in selected circumstances and provide short-term relief, not a cure.

For inflammatory arthritis, disease-modifying medicines may be needed to control disease activity and reduce joint damage. Exercise, food changes or supplements do not replace prescribed disease-controlling treatment. Do not stop or change medicines from this general guide; ask your clinical team or pharmacist.

A balanced diet, suitable activity and support with sleep, mood and everyday tasks can help general wellbeing. There is no single diet or supplement that treats every type of arthritis. Practical adaptations, walking aids or help at work may be useful, depending on your needs.

sections.heading: What should you take to an appointment?
paragraphs:
- Which joints are affected and when symptoms began.
- Whether swelling, warmth or stiffness comes and goes, and how long morning stiffness lasts.
- Changes in walking, dressing, sleep, work or other everyday tasks.
- Other symptoms, including psoriasis, eye symptoms, fatigue or feeling unwell.
- A list of medicines and supplements and what you have tried.
- Your main questions: what type is suspected, what happens next and whom to contact if symptoms change.
A short note or photograph of swelling that comes and goes may help explain symptoms. It cannot rule out infection and must not delay urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Where should you go next?
paragraphs: Use the UK arthritis guide for practical care-navigation steps. Read the osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and gout guides for type-specific information. The living-with-arthritis guide covers everyday tasks and support. Ask your own team which advice applies to you.

faqs.q: Is arthritis just a normal part of getting older?
faqs.a: No. Risk varies by type and arthritis can affect younger adults and children. New or unexplained symptoms deserve assessment rather than being dismissed because of age.

faqs.q: Can normal blood tests rule out rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: No. NICE says suspected persistent joint-lining inflammation can still require specialist referral despite normal or negative tests. A clinician considers the whole assessment.
No. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed without imaging. Tests depend on the suspected cause and examination findings.

faqs.q: Can arthritis symptoms come and go?
faqs.a: Yes. Symptoms and flares vary by condition. Osteoarthritis does not inevitably worsen. A new hot or suddenly very painful joint still needs urgent assessment rather than being assumed to be a familiar flare.

There is currently no cure for arthritis, but treatment can help manage symptoms and function. Some medicines for inflammatory arthritis also aim to reduce joint damage. Your care plan depends on the diagnosis.
No. Exercise can support symptoms and function, but does not replace disease-controlling treatment when needed. Discuss changes with your own team.
